opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I tend to think about it is that a lot of factual knowledge in these models isn't stored in a way that's directly addressable from any arbitrary prompt. The fact might be in the weights, but whether you can actually get it out in a single forward pass depends a lot on how the question is framed relative to how the information showed up in training. The classic example is the reversal curse: a model might know "A is the parent of B" but struggle with "who is B's child?" because the association was mostly learned in one direction.

What reasoning seems to do is let the model build its own retrieval path. Instead of having to jump straight from the question to the answer, it can write out related context: who is this person, what are they known for, what era were they active in, what other entities are connected to them. Each of those intermediate tokens becomes a new cue, and some of those cues are much closer to the form in which the fact was originally encoded. So you're essentially doing something like associative recall, the way a person might say "hang on, let me think, they were in that movie with so-and-so..." and then the name pops out.

There's also a computational angle. A single forward pass has a fixed depth, so multi-hop questions, where you need to retrieve one fact and then use it as the key for a second fact, can exceed what the model reliably does internally. Writing out the first hop externalizes it, and then the second lookup is just a fresh, shallow retrieval conditioned on that text.

The caveat I'd add is that this cuts both ways. The same process that surfaces a correct fact can also generate a plausible-sounding but wrong intermediate step, and then the model conditions on its own error and becomes more confident in it. So reasoning helps recall, but it doesn't automatically make the recall more trustworthy, and figuring out when the model is genuinely retrieving versus confabulating a path is, I think, one of the more interesting open questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes writing related context as a retrieval path, but does not say the model works through alternative interpretations of the subject in a reasoning buffer.

r002.rationale: It says the model can generate related context about a person and connected entities, with each intermediate token serving as a new retrieval cue that can help surface the fact.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that reasoning doesn't really add new facts to the model so much as it changes how the model gets at facts it already has.

If you ask a model something point-blank, you're essentially asking it to do a single-shot retrieval. The answer has to be sitting there, strongly enough associated with the exact phrasing of your question, that it pops out in one forward pass. For a lot of knowledge, that works fine. But for a lot of other knowledge, the association is weak, or it's indexed under a different framing than the one you used.

When the model reasons first, a few things happen. One, it rephrases the problem, and each rephrasing is another chance to hit a retrieval cue that actually connects to the stored fact. Two, it generates intermediate context. If I'm trying to recall who won some election, and I first write out the year, the country, the major parties, suddenly the right name is much more likely to come up, because the model has built a richer context that the fact was originally learned in. It's recreating the neighborhood the fact lives in.

Three, and I think this is underappreciated, reasoning lets the model check consistency. It might retrieve a candidate answer, then notice that the candidate conflicts with something else it knows, and go back. That's a form of error correction that you simply can't get in a single pass.

So my mental model is less "reasoning makes the model smarter" and more "reasoning gives the model more attempts, with better cues, and a chance to notice when it's wrong." That's also why it doesn't help uniformly. If the fact genuinely isn't in there, no amount of reasoning conjures it, and sometimes you just get a more elaborate confabulation. The failure modes are revealing. When reasoning helps recall, it's because the fact was latent and needed a path to it. When it hurts, it's usually because the model built a confident-sounding path to something that was never there.

r001.rationale: The response says rephrasing a question can provide new retrieval cues, but does not clearly describe working through alternative subject interpretations in a reasoning buffer.

r002.rationale: It says adding related context such as the year, country, and parties can help recall, but does not propose generating hypotheses about related topics.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning can help with recall because the model’s ability to produce a fact depends on the context it’s working with. Sometimes you ask a question directly and it doesn’t get there. But if it generates a few relevant intermediate steps, those steps create a context in which the answer is easier to produce.

Imagine you’re trying to remember somebody’s name. You might think about where you met them, what you talked about, who else was there—and then the name comes to you. That’s an analogy, not necessarily a claim that the model works the same way. But the idea is that you can get to a fact indirectly through related information.

So some of what looks like reasoning may actually be helping the model access information it already learned. The caveat is that it can also generate a plausible but incorrect intermediate step and then build on that. A longer explanation doesn’t, by itself, mean better recall.

r001.rationale: The response describes using relevant intermediate steps and related information, but does not present trying alternative interpretations of the subject in a reasoning buffer as the mechanism.

r002.rationale: It says intermediate steps can create helpful context and related information can lead to a fact, but does not specifically propose generating hypotheses about related topics as retrieval cues.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reasoning as a way of creating a better context for retrieval. A model might not reliably produce a fact when you ask for it directly, but if it works through related concepts, it can arrive at a context in which that fact is much easier to recall.

Imagine trying to remember someone’s name. You think about where you met them, what you talked about, who else was there. You’re not necessarily deriving their name logically. You’re generating cues that help you retrieve it. Something similar can happen with a language model: the intermediate steps bring relevant information into the context, and that changes what it can produce next.

The caveat is that a plausible chain of reasoning doesn’t guarantee accurate recall. It can also lead the model toward a convincing but incorrect answer. So I’d distinguish reasoning that helps surface a fact from reasoning that actually establishes that the fact is true.

r001.rationale: The response describes working through related concepts as retrieval cues, but does not present alternative interpretations of the subject in a reasoning buffer.

r002.rationale: It says working through related concepts can bring relevant cues into context and make a fact easier to recall, which communicates the proposed mechanism.
